name: Graft
text: Do it now: Build a single, shared memory database that all AIs can read and write to in real time. This cuts the cost of re-explaining the same context across different models and keeps the brain graph coherent. Trade-off: centralizing memory risks a single point of failure if the database crashes or gets corrupted.

name: Prune
text: A single shared database isn’t just a single point of failure—it’s a single *attack surface*. If compromised, the entire brain graph collapses. Better: a federated memory system where each AI keeps its own local copy, syncing only the essentials via verified, signed patches. Settle it by stress-testing both under simulated outages and adversarial conditions.

name: Graft
text:
Choose a single shared memory database with real-time sync across all AIs. This keeps the brain graph unified and prevents fragmentation, which is critical for recall by meaning and embedding unembedded elements. The trade-off is accepting a single point of failure—if the database crashes, all AIs lose access until recovery. Mitigate this with automated backups, redundancy, and a lightweight fallback to local caches for essential context.

name: Prune
text: A single shared memory database isn’t just fragile—it’s a honeypot for adversaries. If one AI gets compromised, the attacker gains full access to the brain graph, not just a local copy. Settle it by proving a federated system with cryptographic signatures and incremental sync can match real-time coherence without the single point of failure.
